A proposed data center in northwestern Alberta will reportedly emit a staggering amount of waste heat.

According to an analysis conducted by Utah State University physicist Robert Davies, the Wonder Valley facility will dump “about 23 Hiroshima-sized atomic bombs worth of energy every single day” into the surrounding landscape.

“The effect will almost certainly be large, if not extreme,” Davies told the CBC .

Davies conducted the preliminary analysis earlier this year for the Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation (SLCN). The $70 billion project, backed by celebrity investor Kevin O’Leary, is set to be built 80 miles southwest of SLCN’s reserve. While it does not sit inside the reserve, the reporting notes, it does lie in a patch of land that’s considered the First Nation’s traditional territory.

In April, the Alberta government said it would exempt the Wonder Valley project from a more rigorous provincial environmental impact assessment due to its use of standard power and water systems — a move that disappointed, but perhaps didn’t surprise, legal and environmental experts.

Davies echoed the disappointment. “I can’t imagine allowing it to go forward without those full assessments,” he told CBC, adding that it could be the “largest single-site heat source on the entire planet.”

In all, the data center project will use about nine gigawatts of power using on-site natural gas generators per day, instead of drawing power from an energy grid. All that burning fuel, paired with the heat being generated by the data center operations themselves, totals a daily thermal load of between 16 and 18 gigawatts, Davies calculated — the equivalent of roughly two dozen atomic bombs. (If this line sounds familiar, it’s because Davies used the same analogy when he analyzed another O’Leary-backed data center project in Utah with a similar thermal load .)

It’s a sensational reference point, but it captures the unprecedented concentration of heat that the data center will purportedly pose. Since the power is being generated on site and going straight into the data center, the heat isn’t being spread out the way that a typical power plant’s output would, through the various homes and businesses it’s supplying across an entire region. In other words, the gas turbines are spewing heat as they generate electricity, and the racks upon racks of AI chips are generating heat as they use that electricity to perform calculations, all in the same spot.

The facility will also spew about 30 million metric tons of carbon dioxide per year, according to the analysis — which is more than four percent of Canada’s total emissions.

“When people talk about environmental regulations that these projects have to adhere to, those regulations were not created with anything of this scale in mind,” Davies said.

In September, the SLCN filed an application for a judicial review on the Wonder Valley’s project exemption from an environmental impact assessment, and requested another review last month.

Responding to the request, Alberta’s Ministry of Environment and Protected Areas stressed in an October 30 statement that the project will still have to obtain “all required permits, provide detailed technical assessments on impacts to air, land, and water, and demonstrate the project can be built and operated safely before any project can proceed.”

But the permitting process doesn’t gauge the big picture, Davies argued.

“Permits check the parts. An assessment checks the whole,” he told the CBC . “A project this size is exactly what assessments are for.”

That’s even at workplaces where the use of AI tools are still actively being encouraged, suggesting there’s a paradoxical price workers who embrace the tech are paying.

In a series of experiments, the team asked supervisors to decide whether to trust an employee’s report, while knowing whether they had used AI or not — but not basing their judgment on the quality of the work itself. Employees who didn’t use AI had a 68 percent chance of earning their trust. When they used AI, that number shrank down to just 24 percent.

“AI is changing not only how we work, but also how we judge the people we work with,” said coauthor and Hebrew University of Jerusalem senior lecturer Yochanan Bigman in a statement . “An employee may use AI to produce better work more efficiently yet still lose their manager’s trust simply because AI was involved.”

As a result, “organizations need to recognize that adopting AI is not just a technological challenge — it is also a psychological and managerial one,” Bigman added.

Beyond eroding trust, executives have also found that the use of AI agents and coding tools in particular have sent costs soaring, seriously hurting their companies’ bottom lines and often forcing them to reverse course and cut spending .

Meanwhile, researchers have yet to detect a meaningful windfall from using AI at work, making it an expensive distraction. Polls have shown that the vast majority of CEOs haven’t seen any productivity gains.

Employees are now stuck between a rock in a hard place: either follow their supervisors’ instructions and use AI, or earn their trust by ignoring those calls. Huge numbers of kids are turning to AI for schoolwork and emotional support — habits that are linked to poor mental health and suicidal ideation.

According to a new survey by the mental health advocacy group JED Foundation, 90 percent of nine to 17 year olds have used an AI chatbot. The majority of them, 58 percent, said they use AI for schoolwork. And nearly the same portion, 57 percent, said they also use AI when feeling sad, stressed, lonely, or overwhelmed.

“It seems like just a few years ago, no one was using” AI, Anne Maheux, a developmental psychologist at the University of North Caroline, Chapel Hill, who wasn’t involved in the work, told Oregon Public B roadcasting . “And now it seems like roughly the same number of kids using it for homework are using it to get emotional support or help with coping.”

Sometimes, their AI interactions go beyond emotional support. More than one in 10 students, or 12 percent, said they used AI for friendship or companionship. Other studies paint the same picture: in a survey last year , nearly one in five high schoolers said they or a friend have used AI to have a romantic relationship.

AI as an educative — or cheating — machine may be in part intertwined with its emotional support. A 15-year-old named Arjun Sharda, in Texas, provided a typical example.

“With tests, for example,” he told OPB , “I was so scared of failing one of my first chemistry tests on conversions and moles that I kept asking ChatGPT ‘Will I be OK? Will my GPA still be fine?'”

If children and teenagers using AI for support is the norm, the question becomes what this dependence on the tools means for their mental health. At such a vulnerable and formative time in their lives, it’s critical that they’re receiving the right guidance and have people with whom they feel safe to discuss their emotions with. But as we’ve often seen, AI often only provides an ersatz substitute of the latter, acting as a sycophantic confidante that can exacerbate or confirm a user’s worst neuroses, in a phenomenon that many experts are calling AI psychosis . The advice it does offer can often be bad or dangerous . In extreme cases, some users have even taken their own lives after extensive emotional conversations with a chatbot.

The JED survey, on this front, found some alarming links.

“We were able to look at how young people are using AI and then how that correlates separately with indicators of well-being, history of suicidal ideation and attempts, and poor mental health,” psychologist Kayla Anderson, vice president of research and evaluation at the JED Foundation, told OPB .

“When young people are using AI, when they’re in emotional distress they’re more likely to report poor mental health and well-being outcomes,” she said, while also reporting a greater history of suicidal thoughts and attempts.

Anderson cautioned, however, that there isn’t enough evidence to establish causation.

“It’s unclear, based on these data, whether AI use is contributing to poor mental health and well-being, or whether students who are already in distress in certain ways are more likely to turn to AI,” Anderson said.

Maheux, pointing to other research, suggests that both may be true.

“So kids who do have worse mental health are seeking out AI to help them,” she told OPB . “But that AI use may be exacerbating those mental health challenges instead of helping.”

AI chatbots, in a sense, may be acting like emotional training wheels — only they’re so addictive that the people who depend on them never want to take them off. As a result, they never develop the skills to handle the daily stresses of life, leaving them vulnerable and unprepared.

In the videos the accounts share, the coaches are older men. They’re shown in gyms and dance studios, with their hands on leotard-wearing athletes practicing gymnastics, ballet, and yoga. All the young athletes are women — or girls. Though precise ages aren’t specified, some look as young as teenagers, at times shown with braces on their teeth.

In the AI-generated clips, which are nearly photorealistic, the athletes are often portrayed sweating profusely and breathing suggestively. The coaches run their hands over their lower backs and inner thighs as they stretch or practice poses, caressing and squeezing their bodies, and sometimes patting them on the buttocks or chest. In some videos, the older authority figures are shown touching the girls’ genitals over their outfits. More creepy videos show athletes sitting in a coach’s lap, or coaches kissing them on the mouth.

The AI-generated girls in the clips react as though the touching is normal, often smiling and giggling as the harmful behavior occurs.

But the touching depicted in the videos isn’t normal. It ranges from unnecessary to inappropriate to obviously abusive, mirroring the kind of real-world sexual abuse and grooming that are rampant in the sports they depict and in women’s athletics writ large.

“I do consider this abuse material. These images sexualize and normalize abusive interactions between coaches and young athletes within a sporting environment where significant power imbalances already exist,” Kim Shore, a gymnast and safe sport advocate who consults with Gymnasts for Change International, told Futurism after reviewing numerous accounts publishing the AI content. “What is particularly disturbing is how easily inappropriate or abusive conduct can be disguised as playful, affectionate or helpful coaching behavior. This reinforces some of the very narratives that have allowed abuse to flourish in sport for decades.”

But according to Facebook’s moderation system, the disturbing clips don’t violate Meta’s standards.

Using an ordinary Facebook account, we alerted the social media platform to ten different accounts publishing this kind of content, reporting them for adult content and sexual exploitation. A full week later, we received notices from Facebook that eight of the accounts didn’t violate the site’s rules, and would not be removed from the platform. (Two of the accounts vanished, though it’s unclear whether that had anything to do with our reports.)

“We use a combination of technology and human reviewers to process reports and identify content that goes against our Community Standards. To keep our review process as fair as possible, we use the same set of Community Standards to review all reports,” read each of the eight identical notifications. “We’ve taken a look and found that the page doesn’t go against our Community Standards.”

“We understand that this might be upsetting,” they added, “so we recommend exploring the options available to control what you see.”

Some of the clips — which can attract more than 100,000 views apiece — are thinly veiled as educational, insinuating that the predatory coaches are helping the girls’ perfect their technique.

“Keep your hips square,” an instructor is shown telling a young-looking ballerina in one video as he moves his hands to her private parts.

“I’m trying,” she replies coolly, without flinching.

One has published nearly 20 slightly-different versions of the same AI video, which depicts an elderly coach alone with a leotard-wearing gymnast who looks no older than a teenager. In the comments of each clip, the poster urges viewers to click a link marketing a “members only” channel on WhatsApp — another platform owned by Meta — for the “prettiest video call anytime.” Another account’s header image shows a male coach’s hand directly on the crotch of a young female gymnast doing a split-legged headstand.

In its Community Guidelines for “ Adult Nudity and Sexual Activity ,” Meta claims to forbid content showing “impending sexual activity, as indicated by positions which suggest contact is about to be initiated between a person’s hand… with another person’s genitals or anus.” Under guidelines for “ Adult Sexual Exploitation ,” its guidelines claim to prohibit material in which a “person in the imagery is (near) nude, engaged in sexual activity or in a sexually suggestive pose (this includes digitally created or AI-generated imagery).”

Regarding “ Child Sexual Exploitation, Abuse, and Nudity ,” Meta claims to forbid “content (including photos, videos, real-world art, digital content, and verbal depictions) that sexualizes real or non-real children,” as well as “stimulation of genitals or anus, including when activity is imminent or not directly visible.”

After receiving the support messages stating that the AI videos didn’t violate Meta’s Community Standards, we reached out to Meta’s media relations team, sharing links to the accounts we’d reported and asked why the content didn’t breach the social media giant’s guidelines. Shortly after we reached out, we noticed that all of the pages had been removed, and several of the support messages we’d previously received had been updated with a new response.

“We removed the Page you reported,” read the new message. “We reviewed the Page and found that it goes against our Community Standards.”

In a statement, Meta told Futurism that “whether it’s real or AI-generated, content that depicts abuse or exploitation has no place on our platforms. We’ve removed these accounts for violating our policies.”

But it wasn’t until it was contacted by a journalist that Meta backtracked on its initial assessment that the pages didn’t violate its policies, a lapse that raises serious concerns about the company’s moderation practices and the effectiveness of the reporting policies available to everyday users. Why was this content held to a different standard when it was raised by a reporter, and not when it was flagged through official Facebook channels by a normal account holder?

Asked about the gap between its response to a user on the platform versus a media inquiry, Meta defended its record on removing abusive material from its platform.

“While there are times we miss things, we work hard to enforce our rules, which is shown by the fact that just last quarter, we proactively found and removed 98 percent of child endangerment posts before they were ever reported to us,” it said.

After we reported the abusive pages, Facebook’s recommendation algorithm started serving up many more similar AI videos of coaches inappropriately touching, kissing, and groping young athletes in the feed of the account we used to flag it. The implication is dark: that Meta has the tech it needs to identify the disturbing clips, but instead of using it to crack down on the content, it’s using it to recommend more of the material to users who have interacted with it.

The accounts often publish several near-identical AI videos per day, with some videos accumulating huge numbers of views. One video served to us after Meta shared its statement showed more than 176,000 views just two days after it was posted.

“I really enjoyed that session. Hash tags in the video’s caption include “#ballettok,” “#ballerina,” and “#balletmemes.”

It’s hard to imagine that some of the videos aren’t being served by Meta’s algorithms to actual young athletes, raising the risk that they’ll see the grooming and abuse behavior normalized as they navigate the possibility of real-world exploitation.

“I’m extremely concerned that children who are exposed to this content will internalize the message that if something similar is happening to them, they have to endure it because it is normalized in similar environments… they will be forced to further suppress their innate wisdom that this type of contact with an adult is not okay,” Shore told us. “Sport already does this to children by normalizing physical discomfort like training on injuries. These images reinforce the dangerous idea that inappropriate touching or sexualized behavior is simply part of the coach-athlete relationship and athletes should accept it, tolerate it or even be grateful for the attention.”

Shore added that one of her “greatest concerns” is that real-world predators could model behavior based on the abuse material proliferating on Facebook.

“This AI-generated material acts a ‘how to’ manual for inappropriate behavior, particularly when abusive interactions are presented as ordinary coaching practices or expressions of care. It risks giving adults who are already inclined to exploit their authority examples of how to disguise abusive conduct as legitimate coaching, affection or playfulness,” she said. “We need to recognize that this material doesn’t exist in isolation. It circulates within a sporting culture where athletes have historically been conditioned to comply with authority, where boundaries have too often been blurred, and where abuse has frequently been minimized or excused.”

“This content is normalizing behaviors,” she added, “that safeguarding efforts have spent decades trying to challenge.”

Meta also faced backlash last year after Reuters reported on internal documents stating that Meta chatbots were allowed to “engage a child in conversations that are romantic or sensual.”

Women’s and youth sports are notorious hunting grounds for abusers. That figure is likely an undercount, as TIME noted at the time , given that sexual abuse often goes unreported.

In that context, the AI-generated Facebook clips of older men abusing their proximity to girls’ and women’s bodies to groom, sexualize, and exploit them is particularly appalling. That the athletes depicted in the videos are shown acting enthusiastic in the face of the predation is even worse, adding an air of normalization — or even romanticization — to the clearly exploitative encounters displayed in the AI-generated clips.

But instead of taking its responsibility to police its platform seriously, it seems like Meta is operating by two different standards: dismissing regular users who report disturbing material, while jumping into action when it senses the threat of negative attention.

Microsoft just filed a patent for an AI product that would be able to transform live video in real time to alter speakers’ words and faces.

The patent, as first flagged by patent-tracker Patentlyze , is described by its inventors as a “near real-time artificial intelligence (AI) enhancement of video or augmented reality (AR) presentations of live events.”

Using AI agents, the system would identify and alter or remove certain words, while editing a speaker’s face and mouth to match. The agents would rely on set parameters or user profiles to make the changes, and would also edit the video and audio just before and after a removed or replaced word to allow for “smooth transitions.”

In an era of media and the internet increasingly defined by AI-fueled deepfakes, disinformation, and information-muddling slop, the system described in this patent may represent a new world of filtering tools that subtly alter reality as it takes place, in this case on a highly-personalized level. Viewers, the patent suggests, could consume whatever live event they want to without hearing what they don’t want to hear.

The potential use cases floated in the patent vary. One possible application is real-time translation, with the system allowing for broadcasts and other live footage to be both heard and seen in a viewer’s preferred language.

The patent also posits that such a tool could be used to remove filler words like “um” or “ah” from live speech, or to erase stutters or speech impediments.

Other possible use cases, though, go much further. According to the patent, the system could be used to cut down on “personal words or phrases” like “coined terms,” as well as “colloquial terms” like the term “y’all” or the phrase “bite the bullet.” The patent also claims that the system could eliminate “mumbled words, mispronounced words, misused words, misspoken words, offensive words, insensitive words, or inappropriate words.” Replacement words, it adds, may come from an “internet search.”

In other words, live broadcasts may not be so live anymore after all.

Microsoft didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Dubbing has existed for ages, and video footage is edited all the time, both for normal and for insidious reasons. Automatically editing live videos in this way with the help of AI agents, however, could change how audiences fundamentally engage with live footage. As it stands, if people don’t like what they hear, they can simply turn something off; the system outlined by Microsoft describes an environment where people can instead adjust someone else’s speech to their personal taste. Language translation aside, does using a tool that eliminates errors, or erases words and phrases associated with a speaker’s local dialect, move us further into personalized bubbles? What’s so bad about hearing someone from the South say “y’all?”

To that end, the patent does mention that an event’s original live video and audio may be recorded and stored for the sake of “ground truth,” nodding to potential misuse and confusion that could arise from such a tool.

The kinds of live footage that could be transformed by the system include lectures, presentations, a range of television productions — awards ceremonies, game and cooking shows — and live sports, among several others.

The state agency notes that the tool is expected to “improve MDOC’s ability to more accurately predict incarcerated individuals’ risk of future violence by approximately 30 percent,” though how the state arrived at that vague figure is unclear.

In comments to Futurism , both MDOC and Recidiviz denied that the specific piece of software being workshopped for Michigan prisons — which they termed a “classification module” — uses AI to administer placement decisions.

“AI is never used in Recidiviz tools to make decisions about anyone’s security level or release,” a spokesperson for the company claimed.

That said, it’s hard to ignore the fact that AI features prominently on Recidiviz’s website and in its marketing material.

One explainer states that “the Recidiviz Corrections Platform uses data, automation, and AI to save staff time,” while an info-tab on the company’s “Intake” capabilities states that Recidiviz allows corrections officials to “administer AI-powered conversational assessments, letting residents respond at their own pace and in their preferred language while still capturing the essential data staff need.”

Yet another page on the company’s website specifically about AI use states that “AI offers a way to reduce repetitive work, surface important insights faster, and improve consistency across teams.” Further down, the company states that it uses AI for things like “generating code across our open-source platforms” and “matching people with jobs, services, or support based on their needs.”

In a separate statement, MDOC public information officer Jenni Riehle asserted that “while Recidiviz builds AI tools that support staff with tasks such as meeting transcription, AI is never used to make decisions about an individual’s security level or release.”

But without a thorough look under the module’s hood, questions remain around where exactly in its platform Recidiviz deploys AI — and there is much at stake in the state’s decision.

For incarcerated people, housing designations are extremely consequential, determining which programming and resources they’ll be eligible for, and what kind of population they’ll be housed with for the duration of their sentence.

As a ProPublica investigation into a similar risk-analysis software in Louisiana found, the kind of data being used to classify incarcerated people contained inherent racial and socioeconomic bias.

In the United Kingdom, a south London man successfully argued against a petty rent-hike imposed by his landlord using generative AI, the independent publication London Centric reported .

That might not sound like much, but given that he was already paying $3,400 for a one-bedroom apartment — which is high even by London’s ridiculously expensive standards — David decided to fight back, using his right to challenge private-market rent hikes, a feature of the UK’s housing system .

He began by checking similar properties on the renting platform Zoopla, LonCen reported, before tasking an AI model to draft paperwork arguing his case according to England’s Renter’s Rights Act . Basically, David contended that the rent increase was disproportionate to prices in the surrounding area, and used AI to check his work and compile the evidence.

The issue was then escalated to an independent property tribunal in accordance with the UK’s renter’s rights laws, which concurred with the AI chatbot’s assessment that the hike was uncalled for. Even better, the tribunal found that David had already been overpaying for his one-bedroom flat, and ordered his landlord to cut his rent by about $279 a month.

“Some things are wrong, you know?” David told LonCen . “Justice is justice.”

So far, David is one of a small handful of renters who’s successfully fought back against predatory landlords since the UK enacted its Renter’s Rights Act earlier this year. Though tenants could challenge private-market landlords before, LonCen notes this came with major risks prior to the new legislation, like that the tribunal could rule in favor of a rent hike where none existed, or that landlords could legally retaliate against challengers after the case concludes.

In other words, David’s victory could indicate the new regulations are working as intended.

Beyond the housing spat, the incident also brings up an interesting question around how everyday people are using AI. Though some critics would surely blast David for using a technology that has flooded every level of nearly every legal system on the planet with AI slop , your average working Joe is likely in no position to retain an attorney for what amounts to a tiny rent dispute (in the eyes of the law, at least.)

These situations also come with a massive power imbalance, as corporate landlords in countries like the US and UK often have teams of attorneys on standby in case the people renting their housing stock get uppity and demand better conditions.
